This is Maria. She lives in Dubai on a Philippine passport, and she wants to see Tokyo in April. Here is every small step of that trip, and who does each one.
A trip like this is a pile of small chores. Blue is what the agents on her NAS do. Amber is the trip companion, a small program on the same NAS. Green is what only Maria can do.
First, the file agent searches her travel folder. It finds a passport, three visas, a residence permit and a photo of her Emirates ID.
The document agent reads each one: names, dates of birth, issue and expiry dates. Document numbers come back as their last three characters, never in full.
It also compares the machine readable zone at the bottom of the passport with the printed page, letter by letter. They agree.
Her old Japanese visa is only a phone photo. The photo agent reads the text in it. That visa expired in January 2025, so it no longer counts.
Now the rules. The Skill keeps no visa rules of its own, because they change. It saves a one-line research request on the NAS, and the companion fetches the official pages.
The answer comes back as quoted excerpts. Each one carries the page it came from and the date it was fetched.

The Skill turns the excerpts into yes or no checks. Her passport is valid long enough. The old visa is expired. So she needs a short-term visa: about fifteen thousand yen, and about five working days once the application is accepted.
It lists the documents the application asks for, and ticks the ones already in her folder. The flight and hotel bookings are still missing.
It copies her documents into a trip folder. Because that writes files, the NAS asks Maria to approve it in its app first.
It writes the form answers once, from her own documents: every field a visa or booking form will ask. The passport number stays blank for her to copy from the passport.
It drafts what the application needs in writing: a cover letter, and a day by day itinerary.
It writes a calendar file with each deadline, worked back from her flight date, with reminders a week and a day before.
Then it writes the trip queue: research, compare, book, apply and contact items, each with a due date and a link.
The companion shows that queue as a page on the NAS. The page says it plainly: nothing is submitted, paid, booked or sent without her.
For flights and hotels, the companion opens the search pages and saves the options it finds. Maria picks one, and books and pays herself.

For the application, Maria logs in on the visa site. Then she presses Fill this page. The companion types every answer it knows and attaches the right files. Green is filled. Amber is left for her: the passport number, the password, the declaration. She checks every field, then submits and pays.
To ask the hotel for a confirmation in her name, the draft sits on the queue page with the address filled in. Nothing goes out until Maria presses Send.
What's left is what only a person can do: book the visa centre slot, go to the appointment, hand over her passport, and sign.
When the visa comes back, she saves the scan to the NAS. The Skill reads it and checks the name, the passport number and the dates against her passport and the trip.
Every annoying little step, either done on the NAS or waiting in the queue for one click, with the rules fetched fresh from official pages each time.
